William Denius ← Portfolio
Faculty Development · Instructional Design · Pearl River Community College

Good teaching is a practice, not a personality trait.

My work helps faculty improve the courses they already care about — through coaching that respects their expertise, course review that is fair and useful, and professional development that actually changes practice. The three pieces below are working instruments, not slideware. Each one was built to be picked up and used next semester.

See the three artifacts How I approach the work
The premise

Most teaching problems are not knowledge problems. Faculty usually know what good looks like. What they lack is time, feedback, and a structure for change. Design for that, and improvement follows.

The method

Start with empathy, frame the real performance gap, prototype small, and evaluate at a level that proves something — not just whether people enjoyed the session. Transfer is the only result that counts.

The measure

I evaluate against learning transfer, not applause. Satisfaction data is the floor. The evidence that matters shows up in courses, in student engagement, and in retention over time.

How I think about the work

A performance lens, applied to teaching.

I came to instructional design through special education, where the gap between a plan and a child's progress is never abstract. That trained me to ask a harder question before recommending any solution: what is actually causing the gap, and is training even the right answer?

Every artifact here runs on the same backbone — analyze before you build, design with the people who'll use it, and prove the result at a level that holds up to scrutiny. The frameworks below are the working vocabulary, not decoration.

  • Human Performance Technology & Gilbert's Behavior Engineering Model
  • ADDIE and Design Thinking for the build
  • Universal Design for Learning woven through, not bolted on
  • Kirkpatrick + Thalheimer's LTEM for honest evaluation
  • Dessinger & Moseley full-scope evaluation for continuous improvement
Artifact 01 · Faculty Coaching Framework

Coaching faculty as partners, not projects.

A complete, reusable coaching system for a community college teaching and learning center — built so an instructional designer can sit down with any faculty member, in any discipline, and run a respectful, evidence-informed cycle from first conversation to measured change.

Use case Online & hybrid course improvement Cycle length One term, renewable Grounding Adult learning · HPT · UDL · LTEM
Executive Summary

A coaching framework only earns its place if faculty come back for the second conversation. This one is designed around that test. It treats the faculty member as the expert on their students and their discipline, and the coach as a thinking partner who brings structure, evidence, and a fresh set of eyes to the course.

The purpose is straightforward: help faculty make specific, durable improvements to their online and hybrid courses, and build their confidence to keep improving on their own. It is voluntary, confidential by default, and anchored to goals the faculty member sets — not a compliance checklist handed down from administration.

What it connects to
  • Student success. Clearer courses, better-aligned assessment, and stronger instructor presence are among the most reliable levers for engagement and persistence in online sections.
  • Course quality. Coaching feeds directly into the Course Quality Review rubric (Artifact 02): review findings become coaching goals, and coaching closes the gaps the review surfaces.
  • Faculty growth. Each cycle ends with a faculty member who can name what they changed, why, and what they'll try next — the beginning of reflective practice, not a one-time fix.
  • Institutional goals. Documented coaching activity gives the college defensible evidence of investment in teaching quality, useful for accreditation narratives and program review.
Intended outcomes
  • Faculty set and reach at least one concrete course-improvement goal per cycle
  • Measurable change in the targeted practice, verified in the live course
  • Improvement in the relevant student-engagement or completion signal over time
  • Faculty report higher confidence designing for online and hybrid delivery
  • A growing, anonymized library of what's working — feeding future PD
Design stance

Coaching is an intervention, not a courtesy. It is selected, designed, and evaluated like any other performance solution — and abandoned for a better one if the evidence says so.

Stakeholder Analysis · Empathize

Who has a stake, and what keeps them up at night.

Before designing the cycle I mapped each group's goals, motivations, and the barriers that quietly sink coaching programs. The personas are representative composites, drawn from common community-college realities — not real individuals.

DM
Dana M. · Adjunct, online sections
Faculty · teaches two preps, also works full-time
Goal
Keep students from disappearing in week three without spending nights she doesn't have.
Motivation
Cares about students; quietly worries her online course feels like a content dump.
Barrier
No office, no release time, no clear sense of what "good online" looks like in her field.
What coaching must respect
Her time is the scarcest resource. Small, high-leverage changes win.
RT
Robert T. · Tenured, 20+ years
Faculty · skeptical of "the latest initiative"
Goal
Teach well, be left alone to do it, and not be condescended to about his craft.
Motivation
Pride in his subject; openness if the help is genuinely useful and not evaluative.
Barrier
Has seen mandates come and go. Will disengage if coaching feels like surveillance.
What coaching must respect
His expertise. The coach asks questions before offering answers.
PC
Priya C. · Department Chair
Faculty leader · also teaches, also fields complaints
Goal
Consistent course quality across sections without becoming the quality police.
Motivation
Wants a resource she can point faculty toward, especially new and adjunct hires.
Barrier
Can't tell whether coaching is "working"; needs trends, not anecdotes, that protect privacy.
What coaching must respect
Her need for aggregate signal without breaching individual confidentiality.
AD
Alan D. · Academic Dean / DL Director
Administrator · accountable for retention & accreditation
Goal
Move retention and completion in online programs; show clear stewardship of the investment.
Motivation
Results he can report; faculty who feel supported rather than policed.
Barrier
Budget and time are finite; needs to know coaching beats the alternatives it's competing with.
What coaching must respect
The bar for evidence. He needs Level 3–4 / transfer data, not just smile sheets.
Student implications

Students never see the coaching, but they feel its results: a syllabus they can navigate, due dates that make sense, feedback that arrives in time to use, and an instructor who is present in the course. Every coaching goal is ultimately justified by a student experience it improves.

Human-Centered Design & Design Thinking

Designed with faculty, not delivered at them.

The framework follows a Design Thinking arc, and the arc is visible in how the cycle is built. Here is where each mode lives in the actual instrument.

Empathize

Discovery before diagnosis

The cycle opens with an intake form and a discovery conversation that surface the faculty member's own concerns, constraints, and definition of success — before any course is opened or judged.

Define

Frame the real gap together

Coach and faculty member name the specific performance gap and its likely causes. The problem is stated in the faculty member's words and confirmed, not imposed.

Ideate

Options, then a choice

Goal-setting offers more than one path. The conversation guide deliberately asks "what else could we try?" so the faculty member chooses among options rather than receiving a prescription.

Prototype

Small, safe, reversible changes

Action plans favor one module or one unit first — a low-stakes pilot the faculty member can test in a live course without betting the whole semester on it.

Test

Look at what actually happened

Reflection and evaluation compare the change against engagement and completion signals, then feed the next iteration. The loop is the point.

Co-creation

Faculty voice is structural: they set the goal, choose the change, and own the artifact. Reflection prompts and shared action plans build joint ownership rather than coach-as-fixer.

Accessibility & inclusion

UDL is a standing lens in the observation protocol — multiple means of representation, engagement, and expression are checked every cycle, not treated as a separate "accessibility project."

Equity-minded practice

The cycle looks at whether course design works for students who are working, parenting, or new to online learning — the majority at most community colleges, not an edge case.

Gap Analysis & Root Cause

Why coaching — and why not just more training.

A performance analysis comes first, because the wrong diagnosis produces a confident, useless solution. Here is the gap the framework addresses and the causes it's built to treat.

Current state

  • Online course quality varies widely section to section
  • One-off PD workshops are attended but rarely change the live course
  • Faculty get little individualized, non-evaluative feedback on their courses
  • Engagement drop-off and withdrawals cluster in the first weeks of online sections
  • No shared definition of "good" online or hybrid design exists across departments

Desired state

  • A common quality bar, applied supportively rather than punitively
  • PD that transfers — changes faculty can point to in their actual courses
  • Every interested faculty member has access to a coaching partner
  • Earlier, steadier student engagement in online sections
  • A culture where improving one's teaching is normal and expected

The performance gap: faculty largely know what good online teaching looks like in the abstract, but lack the time, feedback, and structured support to translate that knowledge into their own courses. That distinction matters — it tells us the gap is mostly not a knowledge problem, which is exactly why a workshop alone won't close it.

Root cause — read through Gilbert's Behavior Engineering Model

Separating environmental causes from individual ones keeps us from defaulting to "train the faculty." Most of the leverage here is environmental.

Likely causes of the gap, by factor
FactorWhat's likely going onDoes coaching address it?
Information & feedbackFaculty rarely get specific, timely feedback on their course design from a knowledgeable, non-evaluative source.Directly
Resources & toolsNo shared rubric, templates, or models of strong online courses to work from.Directly
Incentives & consequencesLittle recognition for course-improvement effort; quality is invisible until something breaks.Partly — needs admin support
Knowledge & skillsSome genuine skill gaps (e.g., accessibility, alignment), but generally smaller than assumed.Where real gaps exist
Capacity & motivationStrong intrinsic motivation; the limiter is time and confidence, not willingness.Builds confidence
Environment & processNo routine, low-stakes channel for improving a course mid-life. Improvement only happens at redesign.Creates the channel
The honest conclusion

Coaching is the right primary intervention because the dominant causes are informational and environmental — feedback, tools, and a missing process. But it is not sufficient alone: the incentive and recognition gaps need administrative action, which is why portfolio reporting and chair engagement are built into the cycle. Naming what coaching can't fix is part of doing the analysis honestly.

The Coaching Cycle

Nine stages, one term, fully reusable.

The philosophy underneath it: adults learn what they choose to learn, in service of a problem they care about. So the cycle is voluntary, goal-driven, reflective, and built on partnership rather than correction. A growth-mindset framing keeps the focus on "what to try next," not "what went wrong."

Discovery

An informal first conversation. Build trust, learn the faculty member's context and concerns, and clarify that coaching is confidential and non-evaluative. Nothing is opened or judged yet.

Needs assessment

Use the intake form and discovery notes to surface the real concern. Separate what the faculty member wants from the performance gap underneath it.

Course review

Walk the course together using the observation protocol — as students experience it. The coach guides; the faculty member narrates intent. Findings are descriptive, not graded.

Goal setting

Translate findings into one or two specific, reachable goals the faculty member chooses. Good goals name a change in the course and the student experience it should improve.

Action planning

Build a written plan: what changes, in which module, by when, with what support. Favor a small pilot over a full redesign for the first pass.

Implementation support

The coach stays available — co-building a rubric, modeling a discussion design, troubleshooting the LMS. Support is offered at the faculty member's pace, not pushed.

Reflection

After the change is live, a structured reflection: what happened, what surprised them, what they'd keep or adjust. This is where learning consolidates.

Evaluation

Look at evidence — engagement signals, completion, student feedback, the artifact itself — against the goal. Decide together whether the change worked and what it cost.

Continuous improvement

Close the loop: set the next goal, renew the cycle, or graduate the faculty member to self-directed practice. Anonymized lessons feed the center's PD and the quality rubric.

The Instruments

Everything needed to run the cycle.

The full toolkit, ready to use. Open each one — the depth lives here so the framework above can stay brief.

Faculty Coaching Intake Form Stage 1–2 · Discovery & Needs

Completed by the faculty member before the first working session. It is a conversation starter, not an evaluation — every field is optional.

Coaching Intake

Tell me where you'd like to start. There are no wrong answers.

About your course
What brought you here
If you're not sure, that's fine — we'll figure it out together.
Where you'd like to focus
How you'd like to work

Confidential. Shared only with you unless you ask otherwise. Used to prepare for our first session, never for evaluation.

Course Observation Protocol Stage 3 · Course Review

A descriptive walkthrough of the course as students experience it. The coach notes what's present and how it functions — not a score. Findings become candidate goals.

Walkthrough focus areas — online & hybrid
AreaWhat we look atGuiding question
NavigationHome page, module structure, "start here," consistency week to weekCould a new student find what's due this week in under a minute?
Objectives & alignmentStated outcomes; whether activities and assessments map to themDoes every graded thing trace back to a learning objective?
Instructional materialsReadings, video, lecture content; length, currency, format varietyAre materials doing teaching work, or just storage?
EngagementDiscussion design, interaction, active-learning moments, pacingWhere does a student actually do something, not just consume?
Assessment & feedbackClarity of instructions, rubrics, feedback timing and substanceDoes feedback arrive in time to change the next attempt?
Accessibility (UDL)Captions, headings, alt text, color/contrast, multiple means of representation & expressionCan a student using a screen reader or a phone fully participate?
Instructor presenceAnnouncements, intro, tone, responsiveness cues, humanizing elementsDoes it feel like someone is teaching this course?
Student supportLinks to tutoring, tech help, accessibility services, clear contact normsIf a student is stuck or struggling, do they know where to go?
How findings are recorded

For each area: present / partial / not yet, a one-line observation in plain language, and an optional "student impact" note. No numeric score — that's the rubric's job (Artifact 02), and only if the faculty member wants it.

Coaching Conversation Guide Stages 2–8 · Throughout

Prompts the coach draws from, not a script. The order follows the cycle; the tone stays curious. Ask, then listen.

Discovery
  • "Tell me about a moment this term you felt the course was really working."
  • "Where do you lose students, and when?"
  • "If we could fix one thing by midterm, what would matter most to you?"
Root cause
  • "When students miss this, is it because it's unclear, hard, or buried?"
  • "What have you already tried? What happened?"
  • "Is this a design issue, a time issue, or a tool issue?"
Goal setting
  • "What would 'better' look like to a student by the end of this unit?"
  • "What's the smallest version of this change we could test first?"
  • "What else could we try? Let's name two or three options before choosing."
Reflection & next step
  • "What surprised you when you ran it?"
  • "What would you keep, and what would you change next time?"
  • "What do you want to take on next — or are we ready to set you loose?"
Action Plan Template Stage 5 · Reusable

One page, co-written, owned by the faculty member. Small and specific beats big and vague.

Course Improvement Action Plan

Faculty: ____________ · Coach: ____________ · Cycle: __________

Follow-Up & Progress Monitoring Stages 6–9 · Over the term

Light, scheduled touchpoints keep momentum without becoming a burden.

Check-in cadence

Brief touchpoints at the cadence the faculty member chose on intake — a five-minute message or a short meeting. The coach reaches out; the faculty member never has to chase.

Coaching log

The coach keeps a short, private log per cycle: date, focus, decisions, next step. It's the backbone of formative evaluation and the anonymized trend data chairs and deans need.

Reflection journal

An optional running note the faculty member keeps. Even three lines after a change is enough to make the reflection stage real and to track confidence growth.

Mid-cycle adjust

If the pilot isn't moving the signal, that's data — not failure. Revisit root cause, pick a different lever, and re-plan. The loop is designed to absorb this.

Evaluation Plan

Built in from stage one — not bolted on at the end.

Two questions drive every measure: did the faculty member's practice actually change, and did students benefit? Satisfaction is necessary but it is the weakest evidence we collect, so it sits at the bottom of the ladder.

Formative — during the cycle
  • Coaching logs (focus, decisions, momentum)
  • Reflection journal entries
  • Faculty feedback at each touchpoint
  • Observation notes, before and after the change

Purpose: steer the coaching in real time and catch a stalled pilot early.

Summative — end of cycle
  • Goal attainment (met / partially / not, with the evidence)
  • Verified change in the targeted practice, in the live course
  • Faculty confidence and satisfaction
  • The improved artifact itself (rubric, module, assessment)

Purpose: decide whether the cycle worked and what to do next.

Two lenses, one argument: higher evidence beats happy sheets

I read coaching impact through both Kirkpatrick and Thalheimer's LTEM. The meter shows relative evidence strength — the further right it fills, the more confidently the data tells us coaching changed teaching and helped students.

Kirkpatrick — what we collect & how strong it is
LevelFor coaching, this meansSourceEvidence strength
1 · ReactionFaculty find coaching useful, respectful, worth the timePost-cycle feedback
2 · LearningFaculty can name and apply the design principle they worked onReflection, discussion
3 · BehaviorThe change is actually present in the live courseBefore/after course review, artifacts
4 · ResultsStudent engagement, completion, persistence move over timeLMS analytics, completion, retention
LTEM — the eight tiers, applied to coaching
TierApplied to a coaching cycleEvidence strength
1 · AttendanceFaculty member started a cycle
2 · ActivityEngaged in review, planning, and touchpoints
3 · PerceptionsFinds it valuable; confidence rising
4 · KnowledgeKnows the principle behind the change
5 · Decision competenceChooses the right design move in a new situation
6 · Task competenceBuilds the improved module/assessment well
7 · TransferUses the practice in their live course, unprompted
8 · Effects of transferStudents engage, complete, and persist at higher rates strongest
Why this matters

A faculty member can enjoy coaching (Kirkpatrick 1 / LTEM 3) and change nothing. The evidence the dean actually needs lives at Kirkpatrick 3–4 and LTEM 5–8 — decision and task competence, real transfer into the course, and measurable effects on students. That is where I concentrate the measurement effort, while still collecting the lighter signals because they help steer the work mid-cycle.

Impact measures & data sources

Faculty-side

Goal attainment · confidence growth · practice change verified in course · reflection depth · coaching-log trends.

Student-side

LMS engagement & login patterns · assignment & course completion · early-term withdrawal · student pulse surveys · persistence term to term.

How findings become action

Each cycle ends with a short, plain-language summary: what changed, what the evidence showed, and one recommendation — for the faculty member, and (anonymized) for the center's PD.

Continuous Improvement

The program improves the same way the courses do.

The framework eats its own cooking. Anonymized patterns across cycles answer a standing question: what are faculty most often working on, and what changes are actually moving student signals? Those answers reshape three things —

PD design

The most common coaching goals become the topics for group workshops (see Artifact 03), so PD is demand-driven rather than guessed at.

The rubric

Recurring blind spots sharpen the Course Quality Review indicators (Artifact 02) and the observation protocol above.

The coaching itself

Which conversation prompts and which interventions transfer best gets folded back into the cycle each term — a Dessinger & Moseley full-scope habit, applied to the coach's own practice.

Display, Talking Points & Rationale

How to show this — briefly.

Portfolio display

This page is the display: a single scrollable artifact a committee can skim in two minutes or read in fifteen. The front matter stays brief; the instruments hold the depth, hidden until someone wants them. For an interview, I'd open to the coaching cycle, click one instrument live, and let the evidence ladder make the evaluation argument on its own.

  • Lead with the cycle diagram and one open instrument — not the analysis
  • Keep a one-page PDF version for committees who prefer paper
  • Pair it on the site with Artifacts 02 and 03 to show the system, not three loose pieces

Interview talking points

If asked: why coaching, not a workshop?

"Because my root-cause read said the gap is mostly feedback and process, not knowledge. A workshop treats a knowledge problem. Most teaching problems aren't one."

If asked: how do you prove it works?

"I don't stop at satisfaction. I look for the change in the live course and the student signal behind it — LTEM tiers five through eight. That's the evidence a dean can take to accreditation."

If asked: how do you win over a skeptical veteran?

"I make it voluntary, confidential, and non-evaluative, and I ask before I advise. Respect for their craft is the whole strategy — it's why 'Robert' is one of my personas."

Rationale for the design decisions

Voluntary & confidential. Evaluation kills coaching. Separating it from review is what makes faculty honest about what isn't working.

Small pilots over redesigns. Adults change practice incrementally and need a safe place to test. A reversible change in one module lowers the risk of trying.

Two evaluation models, not one. Kirkpatrick is the shared language administrators know; LTEM sharpens the distinction between learning and transfer that Kirkpatrick blurs.

UDL as a standing lens. Folding accessibility into every review — rather than a separate checklist — is how it actually gets done instead of deferred.

Alignment to the PRCC role

This is the job, done on paper.

The position asks for individualized coaching, online and hybrid course improvement, educational-technology support, data-informed decisions, and continuous improvement in service of student success. This artifact is a working demonstration of each.

  • Individualized coaching → the nine-stage cycle and its instruments
  • Online & hybrid improvement → the observation protocol and action plan
  • Ed-tech support → LMS-aware implementation support, offered at the faculty member's pace
  • Data-informed decisions → the Kirkpatrick + LTEM evaluation plan
  • Continuous improvement → cycle renewal and the program-level loop
  • Student success → every goal justified by a student experience it improves

Artifact 02 · Course Quality Review Rubric

A quality bar faculty can use, not just be measured by.

An original ten-category review instrument for online and hybrid courses — informed by Quality Matters, the SUNY OSCQR rubric, and UDL, but written from scratch and built to feed coaching rather than punish. It produces a score and, more importantly, a short list of the next right moves.

Scope Online & hybrid courses Scale 10 categories · 0–3 each · 30 max Use Self-review, peer review, coaching input
Executive Summary

A quality rubric earns trust the day a faculty member reads their results and thinks "that's fair, and I know what to do next." This one is designed for that reaction. It describes what good online and hybrid design looks like in plain language, scores it consistently, and hands back a prioritized improvement list rather than a verdict.

It is original work, not a copy of any proprietary rubric. I drew on the design logic of Quality Matters and OSCQR and on UDL principles, then wrote indicators in the institution's own voice so faculty recognize their courses in them.

Intended users
  • Faculty, for honest self-review before a term
  • Peers and the teaching center, for collaborative review
  • Coaches, who turn review findings into goals (Artifact 01)
  • Chairs and deans, for anonymized quality trends over time
What it delivers
  • A category-by-category score on a clear 0–3 scale
  • "Met / not yet" flags on a small set of essential standards
  • A prioritized, three-item improvement plan — not 40 fixes
  • Comparable data the institution can trend without naming names
Design stance

A rubric is a conversation starter, not a gavel. Its first job is to be useful to the person being reviewed.

Stakeholder Analysis · Empathize

The same instrument has to serve four different fears.

Faculty need

To be reviewed fairly, by criteria they saw in advance, in a way that respects academic freedom and doesn't feel like a trap. The rubric is transparent and the same for everyone — no hidden expectations.

Student need

Courses they can navigate, with clear expectations, timely feedback, and access regardless of device or disability. Every indicator traces to something a student experiences.

Department chair / peer need

A shared, defensible definition of quality that takes the awkwardness out of giving a colleague feedback — and a calibration process so two reviewers don't score the same course wildly differently.

Dean / DL administrator need

Comparable, trendable quality data tied to accreditation and student success — collected without turning the teaching center into a compliance office faculty avoid.

The tension this design resolves

Administrators want measurement; faculty fear it. The rubric earns both by separating the score (for trends) from the review conversation (for growth), and by defaulting to self- and peer-review rather than top-down audit. Accountability and trust are not opposites if you design for both.

Human-Centered Design & Design Thinking

Built the way I'd want my own course reviewed.

Empathize

Start from the reviewed faculty member

Indicators are phrased as observable course features, not judgments of the instructor. The tone is "here's what's present," not "here's what you got wrong."

Define

Name the real quality gap

The problem isn't "faculty don't care." It's that "good online course" has never been defined the same way twice. The rubric is that shared definition.

Ideate

Borrow logic, write originals

I considered adopting QM or OSCQR wholesale. I chose an original, lighter rubric so it fits a community college's load and voice — and avoids licensing constraints.

Prototype

Pilot on volunteers first

Run it as self-review with a few willing faculty, gather their reactions to each indicator, and revise the wording before it goes wider.

Test

Check it against reality

Compare rubric scores to actual student engagement and completion. If high-scoring courses don't show better outcomes, the rubric is measuring the wrong things — and gets revised.

Co-creation

Indicator wording is revised with faculty in the pilot. They help define the bar they'll be held to.

Accessibility & UDL

An entire category, plus essential gateway standards — accessibility is a first-class criterion, not an afterthought line.

Equity-minded

Engagement and support indicators ask whether the course works for working, parenting, and first-generation students.

Gap Analysis & Root Cause

Why a rubric — and what it can't fix alone.

Current state

  • "Quality" is judged inconsistently, course to course and reviewer to reviewer
  • Faculty get feedback that feels subjective or arbitrary, if they get it at all
  • No comparable data exists to show quality trends or target support
  • Accessibility is checked unevenly, usually only after a complaint

Desired state

  • A shared, transparent definition of quality everyone can see
  • Consistent reviews that produce specific, actionable feedback
  • Trendable, anonymized data to guide PD and resourcing
  • Accessibility built into every review by default

The gap: the college lacks a common, fair, repeatable way to describe and measure online course quality — so feedback is inconsistent and improvement is left to chance.

Root cause — what the rubric does and doesn't address

Causes of inconsistent quality, by factor
FactorWhat's going onRubric's role
InformationNo shared standard; "quality" means something different to each reviewerDirectly fixes
ToolsNo instrument, no templates, no exemplars to point toDirectly fixes
ProcessNo routine review cycle tied to anything actionableEnables — pairs with coaching
SkillsSome real gaps (alignment, accessibility) the score will surfaceSurfaces, doesn't close
IncentivesLittle reward for course quality; review can feel like risk, not benefitNeeds admin action
Honest scope

The rubric fixes the information and tools gaps outright. It only surfaces skill gaps — closing them is the coaching framework's job — and it can't fix incentives. Pairing the rubric with coaching and with recognition for improvement is what makes it work as a system.

How the review works

Review, score, then plan.

Review

A reviewer (the faculty member, a peer, or a coach) walks the course against the ten categories, noting what's present and how it functions. Essential standards are flagged met / not yet.

Score

Each category gets 0–3 using the level descriptors. The total maps to an overall band, but the category profile matters more than the single number.

Plan

The reviewer picks the three highest-leverage improvements and records them on the improvement template — the handoff into a coaching cycle.

The Rubric · 10 categories

Ten categories, four levels, plain language.

Each category scores 0–3. Open one to see the four performance-level descriptors. Categories marked essential include a gateway standard that must be met regardless of total score.

01 · Course Organization & Navigation Can a student find their way?
LevelPtsWhat it looks like
Exemplary3A clear "start here," consistent module structure week to week, obvious due-date locations; a first-time student finds anything in under a minute.
Proficient2Logical organization and mostly consistent modules; a motivated student navigates with minor friction.
Developing1Some structure, but inconsistent layout or buried key information; students ask "where is…?" often.
Needs improvement0Content dumped without organization; no orientation; students cannot reliably find what's due.
02 · Learning Objective Alignment Does everything trace to an outcome?
LevelPtsWhat it looks like
Exemplary3Measurable module and course objectives; every activity and assessment visibly maps to one; alignment is stated for students.
Proficient2Clear objectives and mostly aligned activities and assessments; alignment is implicit but sound.
Developing1Objectives present but vague or not measurable; some activities don't clearly connect to them.
Needs improvement0Objectives missing or unrelated to what students actually do and are graded on.
03 · Instructional Materials Do materials teach, or just store?
LevelPtsWhat it looks like
Exemplary3Current, varied, right-sized materials (text, media, examples) chosen to teach specific objectives; sources cited; purpose explained.
Proficient2Relevant, mostly current materials that support objectives; some variety in format.
Developing1Materials present but dated, overlong, or single-format; purpose unclear to students.
Needs improvement0Sparse, outdated, or unattributed materials that don't support the objectives.
04 · Learner Engagement Where does a student actually do something?
LevelPtsWhat it looks like
Exemplary3Frequent active learning and meaningful interaction (student–content, –student, –instructor); discussion is designed, not decorative; pacing supports momentum.
Proficient2Regular active tasks and some genuine interaction; engagement is intentional in most modules.
Developing1Mostly passive consumption with occasional activity; discussions feel like compliance.
Needs improvement0Read-and-quiz only; no real interaction; predictable early drop-off.
05 · Assessment & Feedback Does feedback arrive in time to use?
LevelPtsWhat it looks like
Exemplary3Varied assessments aligned to objectives; clear instructions and rubrics; substantive feedback delivered in time to improve the next attempt; low-stakes practice precedes high-stakes graded work.
Proficient2Aligned assessments with rubrics; feedback is timely and useful most of the time.
Developing1Assessments present but unclear instructions or thin/late feedback; few formative checks.
Needs improvement0High-stakes-only grading; vague expectations; feedback absent or arrives too late to matter.
06 · Accessibility & Inclusion (UDL) essential Can everyone participate?
Essential gateway standard

To score above Developing, the course must clear baseline access: captioned video, structured headings, alt text on meaningful images, sufficient color contrast, and accessible documents. These are the floor, not extra credit.

LevelPtsWhat it looks like
Exemplary3Baseline access met and UDL applied — multiple means of representation, engagement, and expression; students have real choices in how they learn and show learning.
Proficient2Baseline access met; some UDL options present.
Developing1Most baseline access met but gaps remain (e.g., uncaptioned video); no UDL options. Capped here until the gateway is met.
Needs improvement0Significant access barriers; some students cannot participate.
07 · Technology Integration Does the tech serve the learning?
LevelPtsWhat it looks like
Exemplary3Tools are chosen for a clear learning purpose, introduced with support, mobile-friendly, and privacy-conscious; nothing is tech for its own sake.
Proficient2Appropriate tools with adequate student guidance; works on common devices.
Developing1Tools used without clear purpose or support; some access friction.
Needs improvement0Tools confuse or block students; no guidance; barriers to entry.
08 · Instructor Presence Does it feel like someone is teaching?
LevelPtsWhat it looks like
Exemplary3Warm, regular presence — intro, announcements, timely responses, a human voice in feedback and content; clear communication norms set and kept.
Proficient2Consistent presence and responsiveness; students know the instructor is there.
Developing1Sporadic presence; slow or uneven responses; little personal voice.
Needs improvement0Absentee feel; no announcements, no introduction, unanswered students.
09 · Student Support Resources If a student is stuck, do they know where to go?
LevelPtsWhat it looks like
Exemplary3Clear, easy-to-find links to tutoring, tech help, accessibility services, advising, and basic-needs resources, woven in where students need them.
Proficient2Key support links present and accurate in a logical place.
Developing1Some links present but buried, partial, or out of date.
Needs improvement0No support information; students left to fend for themselves.
10 · Continuous Improvement Is the course learning from itself?
LevelPtsWhat it looks like
Exemplary3Evidence the course is revised using data — past student feedback, completion patterns, or prior review acted on; a visible improvement note or changelog.
Proficient2Some recent, intentional updates informed by experience or feedback.
Developing1Minor updates only; little evidence of data-informed change.
Needs improvement0Static course, unchanged across terms regardless of how it's going.
Scoring Guide

The profile matters more than the total.

Add the ten category scores for a total out of 30 and read the band below. But the band is a headline — the category-by-category picture is what drives the improvement plan.

Overall bands
BandTotalReading
Exemplary27–30A model course; share it as an exemplar (with permission).
Proficient20–26Solid course; target the one or two lowest categories.
Developing12–19Real strengths and real gaps; a strong candidate for a coaching cycle.
Needs improvement0–11Prioritize structure, alignment, and access first; coach intensively.
The override rule

If the essential accessibility gateway (Category 06) isn't met, the course can't be labeled Proficient or above regardless of total. Access is a floor, not a tradeoff — you can't average your way past it.

Improvement Planning Template

Every review ends here — three moves, not forty. This is the handoff into a coaching action plan.

Top 3 Improvements

Course: __________ · Reviewer: __________ · Total: ___ / 30 · Band: __________

Sample Completed Review

A worked example — illustrative, not a real course.

A fictional online Introduction to Psychology section, reviewed as a peer review. It shows how the profile, not the number, drives the plan.

Category profile · PSY 1513 (online)
01 Organization & navigation3
02 Objective alignment2
03 Instructional materials2
04 Learner engagement1
05 Assessment & feedback2
06 Accessibility & inclusion1*
07 Technology integration2
08 Instructor presence2
09 Student support3
10 Continuous improvement1
Total19 / 30

*Accessibility gateway not yet met — caps the band at Developing regardless of total.

Reviewer narrative

This is a well-organized, welcoming course with excellent support links and a strong home page — students will know where they are and where to get help. The two things holding it back are engagement (discussions read as weekly compliance posts rather than designed conversation) and access (three lecture videos lack captions, which caps the band).

Top 3 improvements

  • Caption the three videos and run the accessibility checker — clears the gateway, lifts the band to Proficient
  • Redesign two discussions around a decision or case so students respond to each other, not just post
  • Add a short "what changed this term" note and one feedback pulse to start a continuous-improvement habit

Recommended next step: a short coaching cycle focused on engagement design.

Reliability & Validity

Two reviewers, one course, similar score.

Reliability — consistency
  • Calibration sessions: reviewers score the same anchor course and reconcile differences before reviewing live
  • Anchor examples: a short library of "this is a 2, here's why" for each category
  • Two-reviewer rule for any review with stakes; scores within one point are accepted, larger gaps discussed
  • Defined protocol: same walkthrough order and evidence rules every time
Validity — measuring the right thing
  • Outcome alignment: indicators map to recognized design quality and to the course's own objectives
  • Student-learning check: periodically test whether higher scores track with better engagement and completion; revise if not
  • Accessibility grounding: the gateway reflects established standards, not preference
  • Faculty review of wording keeps indicators describing real, observable practice
Evaluation Plan

The rubric is also evaluated — by whether it helps.

Formative
  • Faculty reactions to each indicator during the pilot
  • Inter-reviewer agreement from calibration
  • How often a review actually produces a used improvement plan
Summative & trend
  • Quality-score trends by category, term over term (anonymized)
  • Whether reviewed-and-coached courses improve on re-review
  • Whether quality gains track with engagement and completion gains
From data to decisions

The category most often scoring low across the college becomes next semester's workshop topic (Artifact 03). The rubric, the coaching, and the PD form one loop: review finds the gap, coaching closes it, PD scales the fix, and the next round of scores tells us if it worked.

Display, Talking Points & Rationale

How to show this — briefly.

Portfolio display

The rubric reads best as this interactive page — categories collapsed so a reviewer skims the ten headings, then opens the one they're curious about. In an interview I'd open the accessibility category to show the gateway logic, then jump to the sample review to show the instrument produces a plan, not just a grade.

  • Lead with the ten category headings and the sample review
  • Offer a one-page printable scoring sheet for committees
  • Show it beside the coaching framework — review feeds coaching

Interview talking points

Why not just adopt Quality Matters?

"QM is excellent and I'd happily implement it. But for a portfolio I wanted to show I can build a rubric — borrow the logic, write originals in our voice, and right-size it for our faculty load."

How do you keep reviews fair?

"Calibration and anchors. Two reviewers, a shared library of scored examples, and a defined protocol — that's what turns a rubric from opinion into measurement."

Why is accessibility a gateway, not just a category?

"Because you can't average your way past a student who can't access the course. It's a floor, and the override rule says so explicitly."

Rationale for the design decisions

0–3, not a 100-point checklist. A short scale faculty can hold in their head beats a long one nobody finishes. Profile over precision.

Self- and peer-review first. Defaulting away from top-down audit is what keeps faculty using it voluntarily.

Three improvements, capped. A plan you'll act on beats a backlog you won't. Limiting the output is a design choice.

The accessibility override. Encoding equity as a non-negotiable, not a weighted line, is the rubric's clearest value statement.

Alignment to the PRCC role

Course quality enhancement, made operational.

The role calls for course quality enhancement, online and hybrid improvement, data-informed decisions, and continuous improvement. This rubric is the instrument that makes those words measurable.

  • Course quality → an original, fair, ten-category rubric
  • Online & hybrid → indicators written for those modalities
  • Accessibility & equity → a first-class category with a gateway
  • Data-informed decisions → trendable, anonymized quality data
  • Continuous improvement → the review→coach→PD loop
  • Faculty buy-in → transparent, self-review-first by design

Artifact 03 · Faculty Development Workshop

Designing Engaging Online & Hybrid Learning Experiences

A 90-minute working session for faculty — not a lecture about engagement, but a lab where each person redesigns a real piece of their own course and leaves with one change they'll make next term. Complete with facilitator guide, slide deck, participant workbook, job aids, and an evaluation plan built to measure transfer, not applause.

Audience College faculty (online/hybrid) Duration 90 minutes Format In-person or synchronous online
↓ Download the slide deck (.pptx) See the deck
Executive Summary

Most workshops on "engagement" leave faculty nodding and changing nothing. This one is designed against that failure. Two-thirds of the time is hands-on: faculty work on their own course, with a coach in the room, and don't leave until they've written down a specific change.

The purpose is transfer — a real improvement that shows up in a live course next term. Everything is built backward from that: the outcomes are things faculty can do, the lab produces an artifact, and the evaluation looks for behavior change and student effects, not satisfaction scores.

Desired outcomes
  • Each participant leaves with one written, dated engagement change
  • The change is implemented in a live course the following term
  • Targeted student-engagement signals improve in those courses
  • Participants opt into a coaching cycle to carry it through
Connection to student success

Early disengagement is one of the biggest drivers of online attrition, and it's largely a design problem. Clearer structure, active learning, instructor presence, and access are exactly the levers that keep students in the course past the fragile first weeks.

Design stance

A workshop is a starting gun, not a finish line. Its job is to launch a change that coaching then helps land.

Stakeholder Analysis · Empathize

Designed for the faculty member who has no time.

Faculty needs & barriers

Faculty want their courses to work and their students to stay — but they're stretched, skeptical of one-more-initiative, and tired of PD that doesn't apply to them. So the session is short, hands-on, and every strategy is a cheap edit, not a redesign. They work on their course, not a hypothetical.

Student needs

Students need courses they can navigate, that feel taught, that ask them to do something, and that they can access on any device. Each workshop strategy maps to one of those needs.

Institutional goals

The college needs retention and quality gains it can evidence. The workshop feeds the coaching pipeline and produces transfer data the institution can actually report.

Department chair need

Chairs need a consistent, practical PD option they can point new and adjunct faculty toward — one that produces visible change, not just attendance.

Human-Centered Design & Design Thinking

The workshop was prototyped the way it teaches.

Empathize

Start from faculty time

The scarcest resource is faculty hours. Every design choice — 90 minutes, cheap edits, work-on-your-own-course — protects that.

Define

The gap is transfer, not awareness

Faculty don't need convincing that engagement matters. They need a structured, low-risk way to actually change one thing.

Ideate

Lecture vs. lab

A content-heavy lecture was the obvious option. I chose a lab — minimal input, maximum work time — because transfer comes from doing, not hearing.

Prototype

Run it small

Pilot with one department, watch where the lab stalls, and tighten the prompts and timing before scaling.

Test

Follow the change home

The real test isn't the exit survey — it's whether the written change appears in the live course, tracked through coaching follow-up.

Co-creation

Faculty bring their own course; the facilitator coaches, doesn't prescribe. The output is theirs.

UDL & accessibility

A full segment on UDL and an accessibility gateway, plus a job aid that makes each check a 30-second task.

Equity-minded

Engagement strategies are chosen for students who are working and parenting — short, flexible, low-bandwidth-friendly.

Gap Analysis & Root Cause

Why a workshop is only half the answer.

Current state

  • Online courses lean passive; engagement varies widely
  • Faculty attend PD but rarely change the live course
  • Engagement and withdrawals cluster in the first weeks
  • No structured bridge from "good idea in a workshop" to "in my course"

Desired state

  • Faculty routinely design for the three interactions
  • PD that produces a concrete, implemented change
  • Steadier early engagement and fewer early withdrawals
  • A clear handoff from workshop to coaching to course

Root cause — and the honest limit of training

Causes of low engagement, by factor
FactorWhat's going onWorkshop's role
Skills/knowledgeSome faculty lack concrete active-learning and UDL strategies for onlineDirectly builds
Information/modelsFew worked examples of what "engaging online" actually looks likeProvides models
Motivation/confidenceWilling but unsure where to start; fear of big reworkBuilds confidence via small wins
ProcessNo mechanism to carry a workshop idea into the live courseNeeds coaching follow-up
Time/resourcesThe real constraint — faculty can't rebuild coursesMitigated by cheap edits
The honest conclusion

A workshop closes the skill and model gaps and builds confidence. It cannot, by itself, close the process gap — that's why this design ends by handing every participant into a coaching cycle. Training alone rarely transfers; pairing it with follow-up support is the whole point.

Learning Outcomes

Things participants can do — and we can measure.

Each outcome is observable, which is what makes the evaluation plan possible. By the end of the session, participants will be able to:

Outcome 1 · Analyze

Identify three design causes of early student disengagement in an online or hybrid course, using available engagement data.

Outcome 2 · Apply

Apply at least two active-learning strategies to redesign a passive course element.

Outcome 3 · Evaluate

Evaluate a course element against UDL principles and the accessibility gateway, and name one specific improvement.

Outcome 4 · Create

Draft an action plan with one engagement change to implement in a course the following term.

Facilitator Guide

90 minutes, with the lab protected.

The agenda below carries the facilitation notes inline. The golden rule: if you run long, compress the share-out — never the lab.

0:00 – Open: the disappearing student 10 min

Activity: Hook question — "When in the term do students start to disappear?" Take 2–3 answers. Then the reframe: it's early, and it's design, not difficulty. Show outcomes and agenda.

Discussion prompt: "What about the experience of an online course pushes students away?"

Facilitation: Keep it tight; steer away from blaming students. Drop the workbook link now.

0:10 – Why students disengage + the reframe 15 min

Content: The three patterns — lost, isolated, passive. Then the pivot: disengagement is a design problem, not a motivation problem. Introduce the three interactions (content, peers, instructor).

Discussion prompt: "Which of the three do you recognize most in your own course?" (hands or chat)

Facilitation: The reframe is the heart of the session — deliver it as agency, not guilt.

0:25 – Active learning & the three interactions 20 min

Content + examples: What active learning is/isn't; Strategy 1 (passive→active via chunk + predict); Strategy 2 (decision-based discussion); instructor presence as the cheapest lever.

Activity: 3-minute "spot the passive element" — participants find one receive-only element in their own course and note a fix in the workbook.

Debrief: Take 2–3 examples aloud; reflect back the interaction type.

Facilitation: This activity is decision competence in miniature — note who's stuck for the lab.

0:45 – UDL & accessibility mini-clinic 15 min

Content: UDL in one slide (representation, engagement, expression); the accessibility floor as a non-negotiable gateway; five quick wins.

Activity: Participants circle one quick win to commit to this week.

Facilitation: Reassure — tools make this fast. Point to the Accessibility Quick Guide job aid.

1:00 – Redesign lab 20 min · protected

Activity: Participants take the passive element they spotted and redesign it for real in the workbook: name it → redesign it → check access → write the change.

Facilitator role: Circulate (or visit breakout rooms). Ask questions, don't give answers: "What decision could the student make here?" "Where's the interaction?"

Facilitation: Set a visible timer. Give 5- and 1-minute warnings. Spot examples for share-out.

1:20 – Share-out, action plan & next step 10 min

Share-out: 2–3 volunteers name the element, the move, and the problem it solves. Others note ideas to borrow.

Action plan: Everyone completes "my one change" (change, course, date, signal to watch).

Close + reflection: Two asks — pick your change, sign up for coaching. End on the ask, no recap.

Facilitation: Have the coaching sign-up open/linked. Link the three job aids as people leave.

Participant Workbook

Where the thinking gets written down.

The workbook carries the participant through the session: reflect, diagnose, redesign, commit. Each piece below is a usable page.

p.1 · Reflection — your course right now Warm-up
p.2 · Design exercise — spot the passive element Activity
pp.3–4 · Redesign lab — planning template Main activity
p.5 · Action plan — your one change Commit

My One Change

Carries directly into a coaching cycle.

Job Aids

Three one-pagers they keep at their desk.

Job Aid 1

Online Course Design Checklist

  • Clear "start here" and consistent weekly structure
  • Measurable objectives; activities & assessments aligned
  • Each module asks students to do, not just read
  • Rubrics and timely feedback on graded work
  • Accessibility gateway cleared
  • Support links present where students need them
Job Aid 2

Student Engagement Checklist

  • Content interaction: a decision, application, or product each module
  • Peer interaction: a prompt worth replying to
  • Instructor presence: weekly announcement + visible responsiveness
  • Long media chunked, with a task between chunks
  • A low-stakes win in week one
Job Aid 3

Accessibility Quick Guide

  • Captions on every video (auto + correct key terms)
  • Real heading styles, not just bold text
  • Alt text on meaningful images
  • Sufficient color contrast
  • Descriptive link text ("syllabus (PDF)")
  • Run the LMS accessibility checker
Follow-Up Coaching Plan

The workshop hands off to coaching.

The action plan written on p.5 is, deliberately, the same shape as the coaching action plan in Artifact 01. That's the bridge: a participant doesn't leave with good intentions, they leave already half-enrolled in a cycle that will help them follow through.

Within 1 week

A short check-in: confirm the change, offer help building it. Momentum is fragile right after a workshop.

Mid-term

The change goes live; the coach helps troubleshoot and looks at early engagement signals with the faculty member.

End of term

Reflect on what happened, capture the (anonymized) lesson for future PD, and set the next change — or graduate.

Evaluation Plan · Kirkpatrick + LTEM

Two models, and a clear hierarchy of evidence.

I evaluate this workshop with both Kirkpatrick and Thalheimer's LTEM. The meter shows evidence strength — satisfaction is the floor; the proof is transfer and student effects.

Kirkpatrick — measures & methods
LevelWhat we measureMethodStrength
1 · ReactionSatisfaction, relevance, usefulness, engagementPost-workshop survey, session feedback
2 · LearningKnowledge, skill, confidence growthKnowledge checks, scenario exercises, reflection
3 · BehaviorStrategies applied; instructional practice changesFollow-up surveys, course reviews, self-assessment, peer observation
4 · ResultsCourse quality, engagement, success & retention signalsLMS analytics, student surveys, rubric scores
LTEM — eight tiers, applied to this workshop
TierEvidence collectedStrength
1 · AttendanceParticipation verified
2 · ActivityActive engagement in the spot-it activity and lab
3 · PerceptionsPerceived value and confidence
4 · KnowledgeUnderstands the three interactions, active learning, UDL
5 · Decision competenceChooses the right strategy in a case (spot-it activity, share-out)
6 · Task competencePerforms the redesign — alignment, access review, activity build (the lab)
7 · TransferThe change is implemented in the live course
8 · Effects of transferStudent engagement, completion, satisfaction, retention move strongest

Comparative evaluation analysis

Mapping the two models against each other makes the argument concrete. Kirkpatrick Level 1 and LTEM Tiers 1–3 are easy to collect and nearly worthless on their own — a participant can love the workshop and change nothing. Level 2 and Tier 4 confirm learning happened in the room, which is necessary but not sufficient.

The evidence that actually answers "did this work" sits at Kirkpatrick Levels 3–4 and LTEM Tiers 5–8: the participant chose the right move (Tier 5), built it well (Tier 6), put it into the live course (Tier 7 / Level 3), and students engaged and persisted more as a result (Tier 8 / Level 4). LTEM's value here is that it forces the distinction Kirkpatrick blurs — between knowing, doing in a workshop, and doing in the wild.

Bottom line

Satisfaction and learning data are worth collecting because they steer the next offering. But the strongest evidence of success is demonstrated transfer, instructional change, and student outcomes — LTEM Tiers 5–8 and Kirkpatrick Levels 3–4 — measured over time through the coaching follow-up, not on the exit survey.

Continuous Improvement

Each run sharpens the next.

From the room

Where the lab stalled and which prompts confused people reshape the next session's timing and wording.

From transfer data

Which changes faculty actually implemented — and which moved student signals — tells us which strategies to feature and which to cut.

From the system

The workshop topic itself is chosen from whatever the quality rubric (Artifact 02) shows faculty most need. Demand-driven, not guessed.

Display, Talking Points & Rationale

How to show this — briefly.

Portfolio display

This page is the showcase; the deck is one click away. In an interview I'd open the facilitator guide to show the lab is protected, play the evaluation slide to make the transfer argument, and offer the deck for download — then stop. The workbook and job aids prove it's a complete, runnable package, not a slideshow.

  • Lead with the deck preview and the agenda
  • Hand over the .pptx (speaker + facilitation notes included)
  • Show it last in the set — it's where coaching and the rubric converge

Interview talking points

Why is two-thirds of it a lab?

"Because workshops that are all talk don't transfer. People change practice by doing it once, with support — so I gave them the time and a coach in the room."

How is this different from a webinar on engagement?

"They leave with a written, dated change to their own course and a coaching cycle to land it. The webinar ends; this hands off."

How would you prove it worked?

"Not the smile sheet. I follow the change into the live course — LTEM Tiers 5–8 — and watch whether student engagement moves. That's the evidence that matters."

Rationale for the design decisions

Lab over lecture. Minimal input, maximum work time. Transfer comes from doing, and the protected lab is where doing happens.

Cheap edits, not redesigns. Every strategy fits in faculty's real time budget, which is the actual constraint on change.

Workbook = coaching plan. Making the action plan the same shape as the coaching plan turns intention into a handoff.

Evaluate for transfer. Judging my own workshop by Levels 3–4 / Tiers 5–8 holds it to the same bar I hold faculty to.

Alignment to the PRCC role

Professional development that actually lands.

The role calls for facilitating professional development, supporting online and hybrid learning, applying instructional design, and using data-informed decisions for student success. This package demonstrates all of it, end to end.

  • Facilitating PD → a complete, runnable 90-minute workshop
  • Online & hybrid → strategies built for those modalities
  • Instructional design → measurable outcomes, aligned activities, UDL
  • Data-informed → a dual Kirkpatrick + LTEM evaluation plan
  • Continuous improvement → each run informs the next; topic from rubric data
  • Student success → every strategy tied to engagement and retention
